article.title: The Electoral College bias has returned with a vengeance
article.subtitle: Trump has gained in critical states since the DNC — but that may be reversion to the mean.

extraction.summary: Silver argues that the Electoral College bias against Democrats has returned in the 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential model. Since the DNC began, Trump has gained in the polling averages of most battleground states even though Harris's national lead grew slightly. Silver offers several possible explanations: RFK Jr.'s exit and endorsement of Trump, lower pollster quality in state polls, and partisan non-response bias that fades as Harris's honeymoon ends. Weighted by tipping-point probability, the bias is R+2.4 in the polling averages and R+2.5 in the forecast, compared with R+3.7 in 2016 and R+3.5 in 2020. The article explains how the convention bounce adjustment sits apart from the raw polling averages, shows how the model averages pollster versions with and without minor candidates, and includes a table of win probability and electoral votes by popular-vote margin. That table shows Harris needs roughly a 4-point popular-vote win to be safe, and the model gives a 20% chance she wins the popular vote but loses the Electoral College.

findings.statement: The 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential model applies a convention bounce adjustment. It assumes polls conducted just after a party's convention (here the DNC) are relatively favorable to that party's candidate, so the forecast discounts them. As a result Harris trailed in the forecast of states where she slightly led in the polling averages.
findings.rationale: Post-convention polls tend to be temporarily inflated for the convention party; Silver calls the adjustment highly defensible.
findings.evidence_quote: she’s slightly behind in our forecast of those states, mostly because the model assumes that polls conducted just after the DNC are likely to be relatively favorable for Harris.

findings.statement: The convention bounce adjustment in the 2024 Silver Bulletin model is temporary. As of Sept. 6, 2024, it would begin to work its way out of the model over the following week or two, roughly 2.5–4 weeks after the DNC started on Aug. 19.

quantities.name: time for convention bounce adjustment to phase out

findings.evidence_quote: it will begin to work its way out of the model over the course of the next week or two.

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin 'raw' polling averages are not subject to the convention bounce adjustment. That adjustment is applied at a later stage of the presidential model, in the forecast step.
findings.rationale: Separates the description of current polling from the forecast of election day.
findings.evidence_quote: there’s no convention bounce adjustment in these polling averages at all; that comes at a later stage.

findings.statement: The convention bounce adjustment builds in an expected size of bounce. If a candidate gains less than expected (e.g. 1 point against an expected 2), the gap is minor. Here Harris actually lost ground in swing-state polls, which compounds with the adjustment.

quantities.name: illustrative expected bounce
quantities.context: hypothetical expectation used as an example

findings.evidence_quote: If, say, Harris had gained 1 point, when the convention bounce adjustment was expecting her to gain 2 points, that would look like more of a rounding error in the model.

findings.statement: Silver Bulletin polling averages make no assumptions about whether a minor candidate (RFK Jr.) is on the ballot. They use whatever numbers the pollster publishes. When a pollster releases multiple versions (e.g. with and without minor candidates), the versions are averaged together.
findings.evidence_quote: Our model uses whatever numbers the pollster chooses to publish and averages them together if there’s more than one version (e.g. with and without minor candidates).

findings.statement: After Robert F. Kennedy Jr. dropped out of the 2024 race, he was removed from the Silver Bulletin model. The last model run including him was Aug. 23, when Harris's national lead peaked at 4.3 points.

quantities.name: Harris peak national lead
quantities.context: Aug. 23, 2024 run, last before RFK removal

findings.evidence_quote: Her lead peaked at 4.3 points on August 23 in our last model run before Robert F. Kennedy dropped out and we removed him from our model.

findings.statement: Silver Bulletin polling averages account for differences in pollster quality through pollster ratings, which weight polls, and a house-effects adjustment. Silver says pollster-quality differences between national and state polls make less difference than people assume.
findings.evidence_quote: In principle, our polling averages account for this, with our pollster ratings and our house-effects adjustment.

findings.statement: As of Sept. 2024, Silver Bulletin excludes polls from ActiVote, Big Data Poll, SoCal Polling and Quantus, all of which 538 used. It includes Rasmussen Reports, which 538 excludes. Silver describes Silver Bulletin as more restrictive than 538 overall.
findings.evidence_quote: We don’t use polls from ActiVote, Big Data Poll, SoCal Polling and Quantus — but we do use polls from Rasmussen Reports, which they don’t.

findings.statement: Apart from RealClearPolitics, the more rigorous 2024 polling averages show remarkably similar numbers despite slightly different poll-inclusion standards. Silver implies RCP is an outlier.
findings.evidence_quote: Other than RealClearPolitics — that’s a subject for another day — most of the more rigorous polling averages show remarkably similar numbers despite having slightly different standards for which polls they include.

findings.statement: Partisan non-response bias can produce temporary 'sugar highs' in polls. Enthusiastic partisans, such as Democrats after the Harris candidate swap, are considerably more likely to respond to surveys. Polls may therefore become more accurate when both parties are equally enthused.
findings.rationale: Explains post-honeymoon reversion in Harris's state numbers.
findings.evidence_quote: sometimes enthusiasm translates into unsustainable sugar highs in polls because enthusiastic voters are considerably more likely to respond to surveys.

findings.statement: Silver measures Electoral College bias as each battleground state's margin minus the national margin, averaged with weights equal to each state's tipping-point probability. This can be computed from polling averages (state average vs national average) or from the forecast (Nov. 5 state projection vs projected national popular vote).
findings.evidence_quote: Weighted by each state’s tipping-point probability, it was R +3.7 in 2016 and R +3.5 in 2020.

findings.statement: The tipping-point-weighted Electoral College bias was R+3.7 in 2016 and R+3.5 in 2020. As of Sept. 6, 2024, it was R+2.4 in Silver Bulletin polling averages and R+2.5 in the forecast.
findings.evidence_quote: By comparison, our polling averages and our forecast have it at R +2.4 and R +2.5 this time around, respectively.

findings.statement:
Silver Bulletin lists state leans relative to the national margin (2016 result / 2020 result / 2024 polling average / 2024 forecast) as of Sept. 6, 2024:
- PA: R+2.8 / R+3.3 / R+2.4 / R+2.4
- MI: R+2.3 / R+1.7 / R+1.2 / R+1.2
- GA: R+7.2 / R+4.2 / R+2.8 / R+3.1
- NC: R+5.8 / R+5.8 / R+4.0 / R+4.0
- WI: R+2.9 / R+3.8 / R+0.6 / R+1.1
- AZ: R+5.6 / R+4.1 / R+4.9 / R+4.5
- NV: D+0.3 / R+2.1 / R+2.3 / R+2.2
The forecast's relative lean differs only slightly from the polling average's, e.g. Wisconsin is pulled toward its historical lean (R+0.6 to R+1.1).

quantities.name: WI relative lean polling avg vs forecast
GA relative lean polling avg vs forecast
AZ relative lean polling avg vs forecast

findings.rationale: Forecast blends polls with other information (likely fundamentals/prior partisan lean), shifting outlier relative leans modestly.

findings.statement:
Silver Bulletin polling-average margins on Aug. 19 (start of DNC) vs Sept. 6, 2024:
- National: D+2.3 → D+3.0
- PA: D+1.6 → D+0.6
- MI: D+3.1 → D+1.8
- GA: R+1.6 → D+0.2
- NC: D+0.6 → R+1.0
- WI: D+3.6 → D+2.4
- AZ: D+0.9 → R+1.9
- NV: D+0.8 → D+0.7
State and national averages moved in different directions.

As of Sept. 6, 2024, the Silver Bulletin model gives 88% probability that one of seven states (PA, MI, GA, NC, WI, AZ, NV) is the tipping-point state. Nevada, with 6 electoral votes, has only 3% tipping-point probability.
findings.evidence_quote: Collectively, there’s an 88 percent chance that one of these states determines the winner, the model calculates.

findings.statement:
Silver Bulletin simulation results, conditional on Harris's national popular vote margin bucket (Harris win prob / Harris mean EV) as of Sept. 6, 2024:

| Margin | Harris win prob | Harris mean EV |
|---|---|---|
| D+6–7 | 99.9% | 340.1 |
| D+5–6 | 98.8% | 322.5 |
| D+4–5 | 95.8% | 306.0 |
| D+3–4 | 84.8% | 288.9 |
| D+2–3 | 56.3% | 271.9 |
| D+1–2 | 26.3% | 256.0 |
| D+0–1 | 7.7% | 241.8 |
| R+0–1 | 1.9% | 231.6 |
| R+1–2 | 0.4% | 223.7 |
| R+2–3 | 0.0% | 216.0 |
| R+6–7 | 0.0% | 183.5 |

The electoral-vote response is roughly 15–18 EV per point near the center of the distribution.

quantities.name: Harris win prob at D+2 to +3
Harris win prob at D+3 to +4
Harris win prob at D+0 to +1

findings.statement: In some Silver Bulletin simulations, neither candidate wins an Electoral College majority (e.g. a 269-269 tie). As a result, conditional Harris and Trump win probabilities may not sum to 100%.

As of Sept. 6, 2024, the Silver Bulletin model has the Electoral College as a toss-up if Harris wins the popular vote by 2–3 points. She needs roughly a 4-point popular-vote win to be safe. The model gives a 20% chance she wins the popular vote but loses the Electoral College.
findings.evidence_quote: there’s now a 20 percent chance that she wins the popular vote but loses the Electoral College.

findings.statement: State leans relative to the national margin differ from raw state projections. For example, Wisconsin can show Harris ahead in the polling average while still being GOP-leaning relative to the nation.
findings.evidence_quote: these figures reflect the lean of each state relative to the national numbers — and not the raw projections.

findings.statement: Pennsylvania, Michigan and especially Wisconsin had significant polling errors in 2016 and 2020. Silver suggests that 2024 polls showing a much smaller GOP lean in Wisconsin than its past results are a possible red flag.
findings.evidence_quote: polls show a considerably smaller GOP lean in Wisconsin than in 2016 and 2020, a possible concern for Harris given the history of polling errors there.

findings.statement: Silver treats a state's past relative leans (2016, 2020) as a reasonableness check on current polling. He judges post-DNC state numbers more realistic because they are closer to historical leans, which implies reversion to the mean in relative state lean.
findings.evidence_quote: the new numbers look a bit more realistic than the pre-DNC ones given how the country wound up voting in 2016 and 2020.

political_insights.insight: Democrats faced a large Electoral College disadvantage in 2016 and 2020. In 2020 Biden won the popular vote by 4.5 points, but the tipping-point state, Wisconsin, went for him by only 0.6.
political_insights.evidence: Tipping-point-weighted bias of R+3.7 (2016) and R+3.5 (2020).
political_insights.forecasting_implication: State correlations and relative leans should produce a sizable gap between popular-vote and Electoral College outcomes.

political_insights.topic: RFK Jr. exit and selective ballot withdrawal
political_insights.insight: RFK Jr. tried to withdraw from swing-state ballots while staying on in less competitive states. Voters may follow his Trump endorsement selectively in swing states, which could move swing-state polls toward Trump more than national polls.
political_insights.evidence: Trump gains concentrated in battlegrounds while the national average improved for Harris.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Third-party exits can have state-specific effects that differ from national effects.

political_insights.topic: Demographic shifts and the candidate swap
political_insights.insight: Compared with Biden, Harris gained more among young voters and voters of color and less among older white voters. This hurts her relative position in states like Wisconsin, which have many older white voters.
political_insights.evidence: Biden's numbers held up better with old white voters.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Demographic composition shifts change state relative leans and the size of the Electoral College bias.

political_insights.insight: The honeymoon enthusiasm after the Biden-to-Harris switch likely inflated Democratic polling through differential response. That inflation is cooling as both parties become equally enthused.

open_questions: Expected size and decay schedule (functional form) of the convention bounce adjustment.
How exactly the forecast blends polling-average leans with prior or fundamental leans, which produces differences such as WI moving from R+0.6 to R+1.1.
Number of simulations and how ties (269-269) are handled.
Magnitude of house-effect adjustments and how pollster ratings translate into weights.
Criteria for excluding pollsters such as ActiVote, Big Data Poll, SoCal Polling and Quantus.
